Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): ok thanks everyone for joining, we wanted to keep this a focused technical deep dive on throughput tuning and the kvcache warmup story. Priya is going to lead on the scheduler knobs and the practical runs.
[00:12] Maya (BrightHealth): thanks, alex. Our main problem is bursty nightly jobs plus some user facing prompts that need 95th p95 < 220ms. Right now our p95 spikes to over 600 when the cache is cold so we're trying to get to stable tails without blowing cost.
[00:28] Priya (Redwood SE): yeah that's a really common pattern. quick clarifying q: is your deployment private on-prem? or VPC hosted with a customer-managed control plane?
[00:36] Jordan (Customer): on-prem, air-gapped tubs, we have a private control plane but the inference nodes have restricted egress. we also have a strict KMS policy so any key rotation means a brief pause.
[00:48] Priya: ok that matters for pre-warm strategies; we can't rely on global shared cache. We'll discuss on-node warmup and background prefetch.
[00:57] Sam (SRE): and just to be clear, our traffic profile: daytime interactive ~600 rps, long-tail nightly batch 2k short lived jobs, avg seq len 120 tokens but lots of shorter ones, 8-9% longer than 512.
[01:12] Priya: got it, thanks. so the knobs we'll look at: max_num_seqs (per-GPU packing cap), token_limits (per-request token guards), continuous_batching_window (ms), and kv_cache_eviction_policy + prewarm heuristics.
[01:26] Alex: quick interjection — we often see folks using a two-tier warmup where they pre-populate KV with synthetic prefixes derived from top prompts, then run a low-qps warm sweep. works well when you can generate representative prefixes.
[01:40] Jordan: yeah but for us generating synthetic prefixes is risky — patient data. we need to avoid generating real PHI.
[01:47] Priya: understood. in that case we recommend deterministic prefix sampling from non-PHI templates or using zero-context warmup tokens that still exercise the kv set but avoid content. also, warmup can be sequence-length aware. populate KV with short and medium prefixes rather than only long ones so it helps typical interactive paths.
[02:06] Maya: how does this change the scheduler behavior? does priming the cache increase concurrent packing and therefore more waiting? i'm worried about added latency.
[02:15] Priya: good question. there are two competing effects: warm KV reduces per-token compute so once warmed you get higher throughput and lower latency. during warmup you may see transient increases in queueing if we push many prewarm requests at once. the trick is to use controlled background prewarm with a low priority class that doesn't preempt interactive requests.
[02:34] Alex: this is where the scheduler's priority windows help — we can create a background priority with max concurrency and a rate cap so it fills KV but yields to interactive slots. we can show an example knob set.
[02:44] Jordan: can you detail numbers? like what's a safe max_num_seqs for a V100x or A100-like node when avg seq len is 120?
[02:53] Priya: approximate guidance: for A100 80GB with our optimized kernels and 4-way model sharding you'd typically set max_num_seqs between 64-96 depending on quantization. with int8 quant we can nudge the upper bound, with float16 lower. those numbers are very workload dependent — which brings me to the benchmark we propose.
[03:13] Priya: bench #1: cold cache baseline (no prewarm) with real traffic replay at scaled-down qps. bench #2: background warmup sweep for 10 minutes with low priority then replay. bench #3: continuous warm mode where we maintain minimal background churn to keep KV hitrate > X%.
[03:29] Sam: what's 'minimal background churn'? is that like 1% extra qps?
[03:33] Priya: it depends, but in practice we've seen 0.5-5% of nominal interactive qps is enough to keep hot prefixes resident, assuming your prefix distribution is relatively stable. with very bursty workloads you might need more.
[03:44] Maya: you mentioned token caps — we're using a 2048 token guard currently. should we lower it? some jobs are unbounded and hitting max tokens.
[03:52] Priya: token caps are twofold: per-request limit and scheduler-level per-GPU token window. lowering per-request limit prevents very long sequences from grabbing slots and causing head-of-line blocking. we recommend enforcing a soft cap per request at your business logic (e.g., 1024 or 512 for interactive) and a per-GPU token budget to stop a single burst from using too much.
[04:14] Alex: also consider dynamic token ceilings — during high latency windows reduce token_budget and increase packing aggressiveness. that's something the scheduler can do with simple signals.
[04:23] Jordan: ok interesting. what about quantization? we tested int8 but saw hallucinations and degradation on our fine-tuned family.
[04:31] Priya: right, quantization is a tradeoff. int8 often gives 1.5-2x throughput improvements but can affect output quality, especially on instruction-tuned or finetuned models. our approach is to A/B quantized variants: keep a small percent of requests to full precision model as a canary and run quality checks. for your use case with sensitive outputs, we'd probably recommend int8 for non-critical internal batch jobs and float16 for interactive paths if quality is prioritized.
[04:57] Maya: how does this interact with max_num_seqs? if we quantize we can bump max_num_seqs, but do we need to change kv cache sizing?
[05:06] Priya: yes, when you pack more sequences per GPU, KV memory usage increases. we size KV per-GPU by estimating kv_entry = model_kv_size_per_token * avg_seq_len * max_num_seqs. so if you increase max_num_seqs you may need to increase KV reservoir or set eviction thresholds higher to avoid thrashing. pragmatic approach: measure kv_hitrate and evictions during bench runs and set eviction to keep hitrate above your target (eg 85-90%).
[05:33] Sam: are there knobs for eviction that are safe for on-prem? we can't constantly allocate more RAM.
[05:37] Priya: yes, eviction policies range: LRU-ish time-decay, size-based evict, and prefix-priority where certain prefixes are pinned. For constrained RAM, use time-decay with a relatively short TTL for long-tail prefixes and pin the top X frequent prefixes. That keeps memory predictable.
[05:56] Jordan: you mentioned continuous batching window earlier — what's a starting point? 5ms? 20ms?
[06:01] Priya: typical interactive SLOs tolerate 5-15ms batching windows. For your 220ms p95 target, I'd start at 8ms with a max packing cap that matches the max_num_seqs we discussed. Then instrument end-to-end tail. If your workload has many short requests, smaller windows help reduce added latency but lower throughput benefits.
[06:20] Alex: just to add, our runtime supports adaptive windowing: start at X ms and expand when queue depth increases. It reduces manual tuning. We'll provide a recommended policy file.
[06:29] Maya: and cold start mitigation — is there a recommended warmup cadence? nightly ramp?
[06:33] Priya: for nightly batch-heavy periods, schedule a prewarm sweep 10-20 minutes before peak. For continuous low churn workloads, maintain small background warmers. For very bursty patterns, combine both: a stronger prewarm before scheduled jobs plus a maintenance background.
[06:46] Sam: about measurement — what metrics should we capture in our staging cluster?
[06:50] Priya: essential metrics: kv_hitrate, kv_evictions, avg_pack_size, queue_wait_ms, token_budget_utilization, per-gpu_occupied_seqs, and p50/p95/p99 tail latencies per route. also log per-request seq_len and a prefix id hash so we can map hot prefixes without content.
[07:09] Jordan: ok we'll add a prefix hash. can you give an example of a knob file?
[07:13] Priya: yes, sample: max_num_seqs=80, continuous_batch_window_ms=8, background_priority_rate=0.01, per_request_token_cap=1024, per_gpu_token_budget=200k, kv_eviction_policy=time_decay_ttl=600s, pin_top_n_prefixes=512. We'll attach this in the follow up but it's a starting point.
[07:34] Maya: question on security: background warmup will touch data — we need to prove no PHI is sent to external endpoints and key usage is logged.
[07:42] Alex: understood. Redwood Private supports on-prem with audit logs, KMS integration and HSM options. We'll share SOC2 artifacts and the security checklist. For warmup, we'll recommend non-PHI templates and client-side hashing so nothing leaves your zone.
[07:56] Sam: any known pitfalls with our setup (air-gapped) and the runtime? e.g. building optimized kernels?
[08:02] Priya: building kernels is a one-time step; for air-gapped you build images from our artifact bundle. The main pitfall is GPU driver mismatch — confirm CUDA/cuDNN versions before the run. Also ensure your scheduler preemption signals are routed via the local control plane. We'll send an install checklist.
[08:18] Jordan: about benchmarks — can you simulate our mixed workload? a mix of 70% short interactive, 20% medium, 10% long tails?
[08:25] Priya: yes that's ideal. provide a traffic histogram (we asked for this as an action item) and we'll parameterize the replay. We also recommend running a constrained run where you artificially increase the long-tail fraction to measure head-of-line effects.
[08:36] Alex: question from my side — do you have a cost target per 1M tokens or a max monthly spend? that informs whether we push quantization aggressively.
[08:43] Maya: not a strict number yet, but we need to keep infra costs predictable and within a procurement band. We'll need an estimate.
[08:49] Priya: we can produce a cost delta table: baseline F16 vs int8 vs int4 (if applicable) vs increased max_num_seqs. that'll show tokens/sec and cost per 1M tokens.
[08:59] Jordan: any quick wins we can try in staging today?
[09:02] Priya: yes: 1) set per_request_token_cap to 1024 for interactive routes; 2) enable a small background warmup class at 1% qps; 3) set continuous_batch_window to 8ms; 4) pin top 256 prefixes. Those usually give immediate p95 improvements without big config churn.
[09:20] Maya: ok let's do that.
[09:23] Speaker 3 (transcription artifact): mm-hmm yeah yeah
[09:25] Alex: quick recap — Redwood will deliver: benchmark script and example knob file, security checklist and SOC2 notes, cost delta table, and we'll run a warmup experiment on our side with synthetic safe prefixes. Customer will share traces and logs and spin up a staging test.
[09:40] Maya: timeline?
[09:42] Alex: we'll try to get the first artifacts over by 2026-03-27 and the bench by 2026-04-01. Follow-up review w/ results week of 2026-04-06.
[09:50] Jordan: one last technical: when we bump max_num_seqs do we need to change inter-GPU comms? we've seen higher allreduce contention previously.
[09:57] Priya: the runtime isolates KV exchange from model weight allreduce for most workloads. The main change is memory pressure. Allreduce overhead is more model-size dependent; if you see interconnect saturation we can recommend reducing shard count or tuning NCCL parameters. We'll look at your perf counters.
[10:14] Sam: ok that's helpful, thanks.
[10:18] Alex: any other questions?
[10:20] Maya: no, thanks very actionable.
[10:22] Alex: great, we'll follow up with the docs and the bench. thanks everyone.
